scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: Why fewer steps is regularization: each direction moves at its own speed

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: Quadratic loss, gradient descent from the origin; $\lambda_j$ is the curvature of direction $j$; $\eta=0.1$.

scene-u01-pnew4-50.name: text#50
scene-u01-pnew4-50.text: After $t$ steps direction $j$ has covered $1-(1-\eta\lambda_j)^t$ of the way.

scene-u01-pnew4-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew4-52.text: Condition: $0<\eta\lambda_j<2$ or it diverges. $t=0$ no move, $t\to\infty$ reaches $\mathbf w^{\ast}$.

scene-u01-pnew4-54.name: text#54
scene-u01-pnew4-54.text: Large-curvature directions finish first, small ones are slowest. Stopping at $t=10$: steep directions are in place, flat ones only part of the way.

scene-u01-pnew4-76.name: text#76
scene-u01-pnew4-76.text: Steep directions arrive first; flat ones are still on the way.

scene-u01-pnew5-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew5-46.text: Same $10$ steps: fast in the steep direction, slow in the flat one.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: Compared with weight decay: training less = stronger regularization

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: KP08: weight decay (strength $\alpha$) keeps $\lambda_j/(\lambda_j+\alpha)$ of each direction.

scene-u01-pnew6-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew6-37.text: stopping at step $t$ is roughly weight decay $\alpha=1/(t\eta)$ ($\eta=0.1$)

scene-u01-pnew6-54.name: text#54
scene-u01-pnew6-54.text: Given as a result, not derived.

scene-u01-pnew6-59.name: text#59
scene-u01-pnew6-59.text: Example: $\eta=0.1$, $t=10$ → $\alpha\approx1$: "stop after $10$ steps" is roughly "weight decay $\alpha=1$ trained to convergence".

scene-u01-pnew6-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew6-61.text: Fewer steps act like a bigger weight decay.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: Same toy problem: the two paths are similar but do not coincide

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Orange: $10$ gradient-descent steps; blue dashed: the weight-decay solution as $\alpha$ goes from large to small; the square is $\alpha=1$.

scene-u01-pnew7-68.name: text#68
scene-u01-pnew7-68.text: Distance $0.279$, only $8.8\%$ of $|\mathbf w^{\ast}|=3.162$. Direction $2$ (flat) nearly coincides, direction $1$ (steep) has a gap.

scene-u01-pnew7-70.name: text#70
scene-u01-pnew7-70.text: Close, but not the same point.

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: How exact is it? Compute direction by direction

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: $\eta=0.1$, $t=10$, $\alpha=1$: two bars per group, orange = early stopping keeps, blue = weight decay keeps.

scene-u01-pnew8-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew8-64.text: Small curvature ($\lambda=0.1$): gap only $0.0047$; the larger the curvature the bigger the gap: at $\lambda=4$ early stopping has finished $0.994$ while weight decay keeps $0.8$.

scene-u01-pnew8-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew8-66.text: The height difference between orange and blue bars is the distance between the two ways.

scene-u01-pnew8-88.name: text#88
scene-u01-pnew8-88.text: The larger the curvature, the further apart they are.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: One pair $(t,\alpha)$ cannot match all directions at once

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: $\eta=0.1$, $t=10$, $\alpha=1$: the two "kept share" curves agree only at small curvature.

scene-u01-pnew9-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew9-62.text: To match one direction we must adjust $\alpha$; then the others no longer match.

scene-u01-pnew9-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew9-64.text: So the equivalence is a general trend, not an identity direction by direction.

scene-u01-pnew9-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew9-66.text: Early stopping and weight decay point the same way, roughly equal but not identical.

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: How to use it in practice, and what to watch for

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew10-26.text: Early stopping costs almost no extra computation (it even computes less).

scene-u01-pnew10-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew10-28.text: ① train a short stretch (e.g. $10$ steps)

scene-u01-pnew10-43.name: text#43
scene-u01-pnew10-43.text:
② save the weights
(reset the patience counter)

scene-u01-pnew10-58.name: text#58
scene-u01-pnew10-58.text: ④ keep the learning rate small enough, or gradient descent itself diverges.

scene-u01-pnew10-60.name: text#60
scene-u01-pnew10-60.text: Warning: the validation set also chose the stopping point, so it is slightly optimistic; keep a real test set apart (KP01, KP04).

scene-u01-pnew10-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew10-62.text: Price: validation data is needed, and the "stopping point" becomes a hyperparameter decided by the data.

scene-u01-pnew10-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew10-64.text: Early stopping saves effort, but keep a real test set.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: So far: change the objective, train less; both control the complexity of one model

scene-u01-pnew11-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew11-42.text: Watch the validation error, stop at its minimum and keep the best weights; training less is stronger regularization, roughly $\alpha\approx1/(t\eta)$ (only approximate).

scene-u01-pnew11-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew11-44.text: Common mistakes: "it looks only at training error", "the earlier the better", "$\alpha\approx1/(t\eta)$ is exact"; all wrong.

steps.speakerNotes: Three practical details (added): check the validation error every fixed number of steps; whenever a new minimum appears, save the weights of that moment.

steps.label: KP10 · 1/11 (3)

First see how gradient descent moves from the origin. On a quadratic loss each step removes a fraction ηλj of the remaining distance to the optimum in each direction, so after t steps direction j has covered 1 − (1 − ηλj)^t of the way. Condition: 0 < ηλj < 2, otherwise it diverges. (Added)

First see how gradient descent moves from the origin. On a quadratic loss each step removes a fraction ηλj of the remaining distance to the optimum in each direction, so after t steps direction j has covered 1 − (1 − ηλj)^t of the way. Condition: 0 < ηλj < 2, otherwise it diverges. (Added)

steps.label: KP10 · 4/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The two extremes are intuitive: at t = 0 no direction has moved; as t → ∞ the weights reach w*.

steps.label: KP10 · 4/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Directions of large curvature finish first, small-curvature directions are slowest. So stopping midway means the large-curvature directions are in place and the small-curvature ones have covered only part of the way.

steps.label: KP10 · 6/11 (1)

KP08 said weight decay keeps λj/(λj + α) of each direction. Put early stopping's share 1 − (1 − ηλj)^t next to it: in directions of moderate curvature the two are approximately equal.

steps.label: KP10 · 6/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Then α ≈ 1/(tη), i.e. t ≈ 1/(αη). The relation is given as a result, not derived. (Added)

steps.label: KP10 · 6/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Example: η = 0.1 and t = 10 give α ≈ 1/(10 × 0.1) = 1: train 10 steps and stop is roughly weight decay α = 1 trained to convergence. In other words, training less is stronger regularization.

steps.speakerNotes: One pair (t, α) cannot match all directions at once: matching one direction means adjusting α and then others no longer match. So the equivalence holds as a general trend, not as an identity direction by direction.

steps.label: KP10 · 10/11
steps.speakerNotes: (Figure: the early-stopping flowchart: train a stretch, measure validation error, save weights on a new minimum, otherwise add one to the patience counter, and when it is used up stop and restore the best weights.) Practice: keep a validation set and measure its error every few steps; save the weights of the lowest validation error.

steps.label: KP10 · 10/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: (Figure: the early-stopping flowchart: train a stretch, measure validation error, save weights on a new minimum, otherwise add one to the patience counter, and when it is used up stop and restore the best weights.) Practice: keep a validation set and measure its error every few steps; save the weights of the lowest validation error.

steps.label: KP10 · 10/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Set a patience: stop only after several checks without progress, then restore the best weights; keep the learning rate small enough or gradient descent itself diverges.

steps.label: KP10 · 10/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Note the validation set was also used to choose the stopping point, so it is slightly optimistic about the final test error; a real test set must still be kept apart. The benefit: almost no extra computation; the price: validation data is needed and the stopping point becomes a data-decided hyperparameter.

steps.label: KP10 · 11/11
steps.speakerNotes: (Figure: three methods, ℓ2 / weight decay and ℓ1 that change the objective and early stopping that trains less, all lead to the same result: lower effective complexity.) One-sentence summary: early stopping monitors validation error, stops at its minimum and keeps the best weights; on a quadratic loss training less is stronger regularization, roughly weight decay α ≈ 1/(tη), but only approximately.

steps.label: KP10 · 11/11 (1)

steps.speakerNotes: Common mistakes: early stopping looks only at training error (no, validation error); the earlier the better (too early underfits); α ≈ 1/(tη) is exact (only approximate; large-curvature directions do not match).

steps.label: KP10 · 11/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So far we controlled the complexity of one model: change the objective, train less. Next: can we switch off a random part of the neurons during training so the network cannot depend on any single one? That is KP11, dropout.
